set.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. Santa Clara County elected not to use BHSA for capital development (the plan says MHSA housing funds go to interventions that provide more immediate access) and not to fund operating subsidies with BHSA, so unlike San Diego or Sacramento there is no BHSA capital or PSH operating line to underwrite here. BHSD contracts with two providers for on-site specialty mental health services at PSH developments and will refer BHSA clients to County and SCCHA project-based units through coordinated entry. The Casa de Novo site (Homekey) continues as interim housing. Plan PDF: sccgov.iqm2.com/Citizens/FileOpen.aspx?Type=4&ID=270066 (Attachment B). Audit 2026-11-08 funding_type: classed as grant because the Housing Interventions component funds tenant-based rental subsidies for housing (up to 700 individuals a year); there is no capital line and 0 project-based units, so it is not a development source.

reason: Integrated Plan funds tenant-based rental subsidies for housing, so the BHSA rule maps it to grant; other facts match the plan.

set.layering_notes: Measure E was the City's largest discretionary housing source from 2020 to 2024 and funded many Gap Financing Program awards. Expect limited new Measure E development money through at least FY 2026-27 because the General Fund shortfall shifted $39.2 million (rising to $42.8 million) of homelessness costs into this fund. Developers should underwrite LMIHAF and inclusionary fee funds first and treat Measure E as upside. A Measure E transfer tax refund pilot for qualifying nonprofit purchases (Section 4.59.230) ran July 2021 through June 30, 2024 with one application; it is now expired. Documents read via Legistar attachments because sanjoseca.gov is blocked. Audit 2026-11-08 funding_type: classed as loan because the development share reaches projects as Gap Financing Program loans (the June 2025 memo cites about $60 million of prior-year Measure E and other housing funds for a Gap Financing NOFA); the shelter share is City-operated spending, not a developer source.

reason: Development share is deployed as Gap Financing loans per the June 2025 Council memo, so loan fits best; figures match the memo.

set.layering_notes: Relevant to developers of mixed-income towers (prevailing wage already assumed) and to nonprofit or public master lessees. reason: Memo describes Gap Financing loans and repayable City master-lease investment, so loan fits best; terms match the August 10, 2026 memo.

set.typical_award_size: HCD issued Sunnyvale a Prohousing Designation award letter on May 27, 2025 after a December 9, 2024 application (Housing Element Program H41); the City planned a PIP Round 4 application (due March 31, 2026) for homeless services, outreach, shelter and transitional housing activities (award depends on population base and points; Mountain View's comparable request was $890,000). City-owned site: 295 South Mathilda Avenue purchased September 2023 for $7,325,000 and held under an Exclusive Negotiating Agreement (August 30, 2023) and short-term ground lease with MidPen Housing for a 126-unit project with at least 25 percent of units for families experiencing homelessness; the 2024 NOFA awarded $1.5 million for predevelopment; cumulative City support including land about $13.3 million ($105,000 per unit) before construction funds. The City also adopted a water and sewer priority ordinance for affordable developments and received $1.84 million in MTC Housing Incentive Pool funds in 2025.
set.audit_note: Audit 2026-11-08: kept policy/designation because the record is anchored on the Prohousing Designation; the 295 South Mathilda land is already committed to MidPen, so it is not an open land offering. Designation date corrected from 2024 to May 27, 2025 per the 2025 APR.

reason: Kept policy/designation; the APR shows the Prohousing award letter was May 27, 2025, not 2024, and PIP funds target homeless services.

set.layering_notes: The HOD is Milpitas's main local tool beyond state density bonus. The 2008 Density Bonus Ordinance was replaced by Chapter C.12 of the new Zoning Ordinance (Title XIII), adopted September 2, 2025 and effective October 2, 2025, which follows state law and lists waived, reduced or deferred fees and additional density bonus as case-by-case incentives. Impact fees remain high (about $48,500 per unit in the Metro Specific Plan area including the Transit Area Development Impact Fee, about $29,064 elsewhere, mostly park in-lieu), so fee deferral or waiver for 100 percent affordable projects (Program 20 explores this for specific plan areas) matters more here than in neighboring cities. milpitas.gov opened directly (use curl over IPv4; the www host times out otherwise).

reason: HOD facts match the April 15, 2025 agenda report; reclassed to zoning incentive and fixed the stale note that the density bonus update was not adopted.

set.typical_award_size: The Milpitas Housing Authority is the housing successor to the Milpitas Redevelopment Agency and holds the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund. FY 2022-23 Housing Successor Annual Report (April 1, 2024): deposits $999,623 (loan repayments $75,139, rental income $81,496, home sale equity share $87,064, interest $755,924); ending balance $40,076,469, of which $35,523,352 is loans receivable and $1,800,000 land held for resale, leaving about $2.4 million unencumbered; FY 2022-23 spending $549,926 ($455,406 administration and monitoring, $84,520 homeless prevention, $10,000 housing development). The Housing Element names the Housing Authority as a funding source for Program 16 (site acquisition and predevelopment assistance, deferred, reduced or waived fees), Program 19 (BMR homeownership) and rental assistance, and Program 16 called for evaluating an affordable housing bond or EIFD by end of 2025. The 1432-1446 South Main Street site was being marketed for sale with proceeds to the LMIHAF.
set.affordability_requirement: Dissolution Law (Health and Safety Code 34176.1): at least 30 percent of LMIHAF development spending over each five-year period for rental housing at or below 30 percent AMI (Milpitas reported 86.14 percent for the period tested in FY 2019-20; next test in the FY 2024-25 report); remaining funds for households up to 80 percent AMI; City agreements for assisted units.
set.layering_notes: Unencumbered LMIHAF cash is small (about $2.4 million at June 30, 2023) relative to the $35.5 million loan portfolio; annual deposits run about $0.5 to $1.0 million, so expect modest predevelopment or acquisition loans rather than full gap financing. Milpitas projects rely on County Measure A (Mosaic Court, Sango Court), SCCHA vouchers, Housing Trust Silicon Valley and state programs. Expedited review is offered for projects with more than 20 percent lower income units (Program 16). Later Housing Successor reports (FY 2023-24 and FY 2024-25) were not checked in this audit. milpitas.gov opened with curl over IPv4.
set.audit_note: Audit 2026-11-08: verified from the FY 2022-23 Housing Successor Annual Report and the Housing Element; fund balances added.

reason: Housing Successor Annual Report opened and confirms the LMIHAF, balance and Dissolution Law targets; balances added and source updated.

set.typical_award_size: The 2008 Density Bonus Ordinance was replaced by Chapter C.12 (Density Bonus for Affordable Housing Developments) of the new Zoning Ordinance, Title XIII, adopted September 2, 2025 and effective October 2, 2025. It grants density bonuses, incentives, waivers and parking ratios per state law, and allowed incentives include waived, reduced or deferred City fees (plan check, permit and development impact fees), direct financial aid by loan or grant, and density beyond state law, with additional incentives decided case by case; eligibility requires full on-site compliance with the 15 percent Affordable Housing Ordinance. The Housing Element also states the City provides fee deferrals for projects with on-site affordable units and commits to explore fee deferrals, reductions or waivers for 100 percent affordable projects in the Metro and Gateway-Main Street specific plan areas (Program 20). No standalone fee waiver schedule or dollar amount is published.
set.next_deadline: Chapter C.12 in effect since October 2, 2025. No published fee waiver schedule; incentives are negotiated per project through the density bonus agreement. Confirm with Planning whether specific plan fee relief (Program 20) has been adopted.
set.layering_notes: Milpitas has no local housing trust fund NOFA. Fee relief is available only as a negotiated density bonus incentive under Chapter C.12 or case-by-case deferral, not as a by-right program. Density bonus agreements record 55-year affordability. The HOD rezoning is the other adopted local enhancement. milpitas.gov opened with curl over IPv4; municode code pages are blocked to scripts.
set.audit_note: Audit 2026-11-08: verified against the adopted Zoning Ordinance and Housing Element; corrected the claim that no updated density bonus chapter exists. Prevailing wage left unclear: neither Chapter C.12 nor the Housing Element states a prevailing wage rule for fee waivers or deferrals, and no City policy on point was found.

reason: Density bonus ordinance was updated in the September 2, 2025 Zoning Ordinance with fee waiver incentives; prevailing wage has no stated rule and stays unclear.
